author: reek
body: A Lens model maps raw warehouse tables to governed business concepts. Where Looker describes this mapping in LookML that only Looker can check, a Lens model is ordinary Codex data: records and lists that the type system checks like any other value. This chapter is the modeling vocabulary. It declares the shapes a model is made of and the validator that every model must pass before the planner will touch it. The planner itself lives in a later chapter; the query request shape it consumes is declared here so both sides agree on the contract.

author: reek
body: A join declares its cardinality, and the declaration is load-bearing. The grain checker uses cardinality to decide whether a join can fan rows out and therefore whether a naive aggregate would double-count. ManyToOne is the workhorse: many fact rows point at one dimension row, and an aggregate computed at the fact table's own grain stays correct across the join. The other two directions are declared now and exploited by the planner later.

author: reek
body: Every measure names the aggregate that summarizes it. The five kinds below cover the LookML core. The constructors carry a Lens prefix rather than the bare names AggSum through AggMax because the Data quire's RelAlgebra chapter already owns those constructor names, and constructor names are program-wide: the planner will cite both chapters in one program, so the bare names would collide.

author: reek
body: A LensTable points the model at one physical table. The primary key is what makes grain reasoning possible: a many-to-one join is only trustworthy when the one side can be identified row by row. The grain field is prose for the analyst, one honest sentence about what a single row means.

author: reek
body: A LensJoin relates two declared tables by one column on each side. The cardinality field is not documentation. The validator checks that a many-to-one join's destination declares a primary key, and the grain checker will refuse plans that fan out through it.

author: reek
body: A dimension may bucket a date column by calendar period: year, quarter, month, or day. Dates are Unix seconds stored in integer columns by convention, and declaring a bucket is the modeler's assertion that the column holds Unix seconds; the validator does not police that assertion, in the same manner it does not police that an amount column holds cents. The constructors carry an Lb prefix because constructor names are program-wide and the bare calendar words are too valuable to claim. LbNone means the dimension reads its column as-is, which is every dimension that existed before buckets did.

author: reek
body: A dimension is an attribute column that segments the data. It names its home table, the column it reads, and the bucket that column is read through.

author: reek
body: A measure is a governed aggregate: a column on a home table, an aggregation kind, and a description that a controller can sign off on. Measure filters are deferred. A filter needs a predicate type, and inventing one here would prejudge the planner's expression language. When the predicate type exists, filters become one more field on this record.

author: reek
body: A LensModel gathers the whole vocabulary under one name. This value is the unit of validation, the unit of versioning, and the ground the planner stands on.

author: reek
body: A query filter is an equality test: one column on one table must equal one literal value. The value is its own small sum so the filter mirrors the relational predicate's column-versus-literal shape without citing the engine: an integer or a text, nothing else in v1. The planner places each filter at raw-row grain, under the aggregations, therefore a filter can never see a summed row.

author: reek
body: A LensQuery is the request shape the planner consumes: which lens to ask, which dimensions to group by, which measures to compute, the filters to apply before any aggregation, and a row limit. Dimension and measure names refer to the model's declared dimensions and measures, never to raw columns; filters name physical tables and columns and the planner checks them against the model's vocabulary.

author: reek
body: Validation reports diagnostics as code plus message. Codes are app-level, drawn from the 1 to 99 range, and are not compiler CDX codes. The table:

author: reek
body: code 1 means a table name is declared more than once. code 2 means a join's from-table is not a declared table. code 3 means a join's to-table is not a declared table. code 4 means a many-to-one join's to-table declares no primary key. code 5 means a dimension's table is not a declared table. code 6 means a measure's table is not a declared table. code 7 means a measure name is declared more than once.

author: reek
body: Two small scans over the declared tables. Both walk by index with an explicit stop, so the duplicate check can reuse the same walk to ask whether a name appears before a given position.

author: reek
body: lens-validate is the gate between a model as written and a model the planner may plan against. It threads one diagnostic accumulator through four passes: duplicate tables, joins, dimensions, measures. A clean model yields the empty list.

author: reek
body: Each join is checked three ways: its from-table must be declared, its to-table must be declared, and when the join is many-to-one its to-table must carry a nonempty primary key, because grain checking identifies the one side by that key. The key check is skipped when the to-table is itself undeclared; code 3 already tells that story.

author: reek
body: Dimensions and measures must live on declared tables, and measure names must be unique because the query surface addresses measures by name alone.
